scenes.title: Late for his miracle
paragraphs: Blaise was late for his own miracle.

The guests had already taken the good chairs. Through the palace windows he could see the theatre across the square, its long window propped open with a piece of scenery. Something enormous and white moved inside. Julian had said he would only need help for an hour. That had been an hour ago.

Erasmus came toward Blaise carrying two cups and a plate balanced on one forearm. He managed this well. It was one of the things that made his power difficult to place. A man who could restore the city still took a visible satisfaction in bringing three things across a crowded room without a tray.
“You've come without the robe,” he said.
“Julian needs it.”
“You will be able to speak without it, I hope.”
Blaise took a cup. The liquid had tiny lights in it. Above the highest terrace the night had left several stars close enough to reach, and Erasmus's kitchen had been experimenting.
“They don't dissolve,” the patron said. “You can leave it in the bottom.”

The commemorative cloth hung behind the table. Blaise recognized the bridge in its embroidery, the fall of white stone, the small human shape somebody had made for him beneath it. On the other side stood an uninjured figure under an ascending sun. Whoever had sewn it had given the restored man larger hands.
“I wasn't so graceful,” Blaise said.
“You needn't describe the injury. Tell them why you think you were brought back.”
“Because Julian asked.”
“And why his request was answered.”
The guests had noticed him. A child was being moved from a chair so that Blaise could sit at the center. He could no longer pretend that this was merely a meal at which an old subject might arise.

He owed Erasmus his life. He could say that without qualification. What troubled him was the movement from owing his life to knowing what the life was for. The patron's attention had made the transition seem natural. Blaise had survived; somebody wanted him to survive; perhaps therefore he had been necessary to a purpose he could not yet see.
He wanted that conclusion. It would have been pleasant to stand before a room of people and discover that gratitude had made him important.
Across the square, Julian's white object struck the inside of the theatre window. Blaise heard a very distant swear.
“I told them you would explain,” Erasmus said.

choices.label: Say that you can thank Erasmus but cannot claim to know why you were chosen.
Tell Erasmus you will not turn the injury into this performance.

scenes.title: The part he cannot say
paragraphs: “I can tell them what you did,” Blaise said. “I can't tell them what it proves about the reason I exist.”
Erasmus held the plate between them. Blaise took a piece of bread because it seemed rude to leave him holding it.
“You believe there was a reason.”
“I want there to have been.”
“You say that as though wanting were an objection.”
“It isn't an answer either.”
The patron looked toward the guests. The child was still being persuaded to surrender the chair. Erasmus set the plate down and told the parent to leave the child where she was.

choices.label: Remain while Erasmus tells the guests.

scenes.title: A different audience
paragraphs: “I don't want them to watch me remember being crushed,” Blaise said.
“That isn't what I asked.”
“It is what you put on the cloth.”
Erasmus looked back at it. The embroidered figure lay patiently beneath the falling stone.
“You might have said so before they arrived.”
“You might have asked before inviting them.”

Blaise wished at once that he had found a way to say it which would not sound so satisfactory when repeated. Some of the guests had heard. He could feel their attention becoming the thing he had objected to.
Erasmus set down the plate and went to the center of the room.

choices.label: Remain while Erasmus tells the guests.

scenes.title: The cloth comes down
paragraphs: “There will be no address,” Erasmus said. “Please eat.”
One of the guests began to object on Blaise's behalf. Erasmus interrupted before the objection had acquired a purpose. He asked a different guest about her journey, then went to take down the cloth.
It caught on one of its hooks. Blaise moved to help.
“I can manage this.”
The patron tugged too hard. A loop tore, and the restored figure folded over the injured one. Erasmus held the fabric while he worked the remaining loop free.

For a moment Blaise could almost see how the scene might have gone better. He could have arrived earlier, thanked him privately, refused with more tenderness. Gratitude might have survived without that torn sound. He caught himself considering an arrangement of events which would let him say no without making another person experience refusal.
Erasmus carried the cloth into the passage. Blaise followed him as far as the door.
“Will you be angry all day?” he asked.
“I don't yet know.”
“You could know.”
The patron stopped folding.
“I promised you something when you came back. While you remain in Aubade I will not return the city without your request. I have not revoked it.”
“Even for this?”
“Especially if the purpose were to have a more agreeable conversation.”
Blaise heard a reproach in it. Erasmus did not say whose earlier requests he had in mind.
“Go and help Julian,” the patron said. “He has been making a distressing amount of noise.”

Outside, the street rose away from the square, turning gradually until its upper houses hung over the lower ones. Somebody leaned out high above Blaise to shake a rug. Dust climbed past them both toward the dark curve of the sky.

choices.label: Cross the square to help Julian.

scenes.title: The horse's other end
paragraphs: Blaise caught the horse's leg before it fell.
Julian remained inside the horse, swearing. From the wardrobe came the scrape of paper against paper, then a soft tearing sound.
“Don't pull,” Blaise said.
“I am trying to become smaller.”

The theatre had been a dining room. Its long window looked across the square at a street that climbed steadily until the houses hung above their own roofs. Someone on the upper terrace was beating a rug. Dust rose through the window instead of settling, and Julian had spent the morning trying to keep it out of the wet paint.

Blaise set the leg against the wall. He held the wardrobe door open and took the horse by its enormous chin. Julian crawled backward, bringing out a pair of human feet first, then the other three legs, then a mane made from the fringe of Erasmus's discarded dressing gown.
“I measured it,” Julian said.
“The wardrobe?”
“The head.”
Blaise laughed.
Julian's shoulders stopped moving.
“That wasn't the funny part.”
“It was quite good.”
“No. I was going to say I forgot about the horse's other end.”
“That is better.”
Julian waited. Blaise could have laughed again. He had done so once before, a short, embarrassed sound which made the rest of the afternoon unpleasant. Instead he bent to retrieve the fallen leg.

It had come off in his hand this time. Previously it had struck Julian's ankle. Anticipating something was not always an offence. He had prevented an injury, although Julian would laugh at the grandeur of that description. An ankle bumped by paper. A little less pain in the world. Surely he was allowed that.
Julian took the leg from him.
“Thank you.”
He said it without irony. The relief was so immediate that Blaise wanted to thank him for it.

They mended the horse at the long table. Julian held the joint while Blaise wound string around it. Beneath the paper, the wooden ribs were visible. Julian had written figures on one of them, crossed them out, then written the same figures larger.
“I see you checked your measurements.”
“I checked my confidence.”
This time Blaise laughed at the right moment.

choices.label: Stay beside Julian as they mend the horse.

scenes.title: A useful animal
paragraphs: Julian leaned against him to reach the scissors. Blaise let his hand rest on the back of Julian's neck. A little dried paint came away beneath his thumb. He liked Julian like this, occupied and warm, impatient with an object which had refused to become exactly what he imagined. Julian turned and kissed him, then took the scissors from behind his elbow.
Nothing had been extracted from him. Blaise had not supplied the required phrase. He had been standing there, holding a piece of string, and Julian had wanted to kiss him.

But he had stood where Julian would reach across him. Had he known that? His memory contained so many small arrangements that he could no longer reliably separate an anticipation from a wish. Perhaps the kiss had followed because Julian was grateful for the repaired horse, because Blaise had laughed, because he was accustomed to finding him agreeable at this hour.
Why did discovering a cause always feel like discovering a substitute?

If Julian had kissed him for no reason, the act would have belonged to nobody. A twitch could have done as much. Blaise wanted the kiss to follow from Julian's affection, from the particular man who had been here yesterday. Yet once he had given the affection a history, he found himself looking behind it for something that the history had not produced.

He was easy to love because he was useful, perhaps. Or because he was funny. A funnier, more useful man could then stand in his place. The conditions would be satisfied; the world would proceed without noticing the exchange.
Julian was turning the scissors in his hand.
“You're pulling,” he said.
Blaise released the string.
“Sorry.”
“I like the leg attached. It makes the marriage possible.”
The horse was to marry a judge in the last scene. The play had once concerned a dispute over an orchard. Julian had become bored with the orchard.
He fetched Blaise's robe from the back of a chair. It was a curtain with sleeves.
“Just the entrance. I need to know how long it takes you to get around the table.”
“Dignity cannot be hurried.”
“Dignity can go around the other side.”
Blaise put on the robe. It trailed behind him for several feet. He stood very still, then lifted a hand as though granting the furniture permission to exist.
Julian's breathing changed. Blaise heard the laugh he was trying to prevent and prolonged the gesture.
“Your Honour,” Julian said, and failed to go on.
Blaise bowed to the horse.
“I have considered your proposal. My advisers are concerned about the disparity in our stations.”
“He's a judge too,” Julian managed.
“Then I withdraw my objection to his eating them.”

Julian sat on the table. He was laughing properly now, one hand pressed flat against the wood. Blaise went around the room with such delicate solemnity that the hem caught beneath his heel. He recovered, pretended that the stumble was a bow and heard Julian laugh harder.
He wanted to do the whole scene. He wanted Julian to remain there until evening, unable to ask him for anything except another line.
“Keep that,” Julian said. “The bow.”
“And the advisers?”
“The advisers can go. I like you falling over.”
Blaise made an injured sound and gathered up the robe's long hem.

choices.label: Ask about the folded letter beside the paint.

scenes.title: A place elsewhere
paragraphs: Julian had stopped laughing. He was looking at a folded letter beside the paint pot.
“They've made the roof high enough,” he said.
“Who has?”
“The company I told you about. Beyond the west road.”
“You told me they hadn't decided where to put the stage.”
“They hadn't then.”
There was a drawing inside the letter. A black wall of rain rose behind a narrow platform. Somebody had added a horse much too large for it.
“They've seen your measurements,” Blaise said.
“I drew the horse.”
Julian smoothed the paper against the table.
“I told them you might do the judge.”
“Might?”
“I told them you'd do it. I shouldn't have. I've written back.”
“What did you tell them this time?”
“That I would ask you.”
Blaise waited for the question. Julian did not ask it.
Outside, the rug-beater had stopped. A loose thread drifted upward past the window, curling toward the dark underside of the street.
“I thought you were happy here,” Blaise said.
“I am, sometimes.”
“You said you were.”
“Yes.”
There was no embarrassment in the answer. Julian seemed to think he could admit having been happy without conceding anything about what he owed to that happiness.
“I don't understand what has changed.”
“I want to see what happens to the play after somebody sees it.”
“People can see it here.”
“And afterward?”
Blaise looked at the letter. The drawn rain had been made with hundreds of little strokes. Someone had spent an afternoon on a place neither of them had visited together.
“Erasmus doesn't return the city every night,” he said.
“How often does he?”
“When somebody needs him to.”
“That wasn't what I asked.”
Julian put the letter away. He did not slam a drawer or turn his back. He remained beside Blaise, close enough that the edge of his sleeve touched his hand.
“I asked him once,” Julian said. “I know what it can mean to need it.”

Blaise remembered the bridge coming down. Less the impact than the small white piece of sky visible between Julian's fingers. Julian had been holding something against his chest. He had kept saying Blaise's name as though the repetition itself could prevent the thing it named from disappearing.

They had wanted the morning. Both of them. Afterward they had sat on the unbroken bridge, eating bread, and Julian had become angry because Blaise said they ought to go and do something with the day. For an hour, Julian wanted to do nothing at all.
Was that wish worth less because it came before this one?

If the later Julian could overrule the earlier, then tomorrow's wish could overrule this departure too. Why should Blaise cooperate in destroying a happiness merely because its opponent was speaking last? There was no virtue in lateness. A cruel impulse could arrive after a generous one. Discovery could improve a judgment; fatigue could spoil it. Time did not adjudicate between them.
Erasmus remembered both. Perhaps that was what Blaise needed from him: a judgment which did not mistake the order of desires for their worth.
Then he noticed where his thought had taken him. He wanted Erasmus to decide which Julian was entitled to answer. Naturally he hoped the entitled one would love him best.
The hope did not make the argument false. That was the refuge he always reached. A hungry man could correctly identify bread. Wanting a thing did not refute the reasons for wanting it.
“I want you to come,” Julian said.
Blaise had been preparing to oppose a departure in which he had no place. The invitation made him feel strangely cheated.
“And if I don't?”
Julian rubbed a little dried glue between his fingers. It came away in a translucent curl.
“I think I'll go.”

He could ask what Julian had meant by bringing him back if he was only going to leave. Once, that question had brought Julian across the room. Blaise remembered the relief of feeling him kneel against his legs, and how carefully he had avoided mentioning the question afterward.
He said, “Help me out of this thing.”

The curtain had twisted around his waist. Julian untied it. For a moment his arms encircled Blaise from behind. Blaise shut his eyes and allowed himself the contact without saying anything that would make Julian account for it.
“We haven't tried the final speech,” Julian said.
“You haven't finished it.”
“I have something.”

scenes.title: The word on the back
paragraphs: He fetched the pages and gave Blaise the top one.
The judge had lost his office, his house and the horse. At the bottom of the page he announced that he would remain where he was until the roses apologized.
Blaise remembered Julian reading it to him in bed. The line had not worked. Together they had changed it.
“Until the roses admit they were weeds,” Blaise said.
Julian became very still.
The silence was new. Blaise had no account of how long it would last.
“What?” Julian said.
“It's funnier.”
“I know it's funnier.”
“You told me there hadn't been another return while we were writing this.”
Julian took the page. On the back was a single word, written small enough to hide beneath his thumb.
Blaise could not see it. He knew what it was.
“Did you look?”
“At what?”
Julian turned the paper over. Weeds.
It would have been easy to say yes. A little intrusion, immediately forgivable. Blaise could confess to looking through Julian's pages and receive the anger due to a much smaller act.
“No,” he said.
Julian waited.

Blaise wanted to explain the evening in bed, the warm place at his back, how much he had loved helping to make the line. To Julian it would be a thing Blaise had taken from a future he had not been permitted to reach. To Blaise it was something they had done together. He could not make himself call it theft without also seeming to deny that it had been theirs.
Julian folded the page once.
“I'm taking the door to Vera.”
“Why?”
“She said she'd help me paint the sky on the other side.”
“Now?”
“While it's light.”
He went to the painted door at the rear of the stage and lifted it from its loose hinges. The horse was in his way. Blaise moved it aside.
Julian paused with the door against his shoulder.
“You could tell me,” he said.
Blaise looked down at the robe on the floor. He could still hear the afternoon in which Julian had laughed at the revised line. It remained a fact. No amount of fear could make it not have happened.
“It was ours,” he said.
Julian adjusted his grip and carried the door outside.

choices.label: Remain in the theatre after Julian leaves.

scenes.title: An opening in the scenery
paragraphs: The cupboard behind the removed door was full of things Julian had not found a use for. A broken umbrella. A strip of red cloth. The first attempt at the horse's head, which was small enough to suggest that some entirely different animal had once been considered.
Blaise sat on the table. He wanted Julian to come back and ask the question again in a way that made the answer possible.

He could have followed him. Vera kept her instruments near the western edge. Julian had said where he was going. There was nothing mysterious about the route, nothing which required a favor before Blaise could take it.
Instead he picked up the page.
Weeds.

He could remember the pleasure with which they had reached that word. It was not a story Erasmus had told him. Julian had been lying on his stomach with a pencil under his hand, and Blaise had watched him make the small alteration. Afterward they had done nothing important. The evening remained valuable without having produced a declaration or an explanation.
He had brought the word into this afternoon as though carrying something safely out of a fire. Julian had experienced it as a hand inside a drawer.

Blaise put the page down. Through the open window he saw the cart pass the corner of the square. The painted door lay flat across it. Julian was walking beside the horse, making room for something that had once filled their room together.
The cart did not turn toward the edge where Vera worked. It continued to the west road.
Blaise went to the palace.

choices.label: Tell Erasmus plainly that Julian appears to be leaving.
Tell Erasmus that the afternoon has been ruined.

scenes.title: The person who remembers
paragraphs: Erasmus was eating in the kitchen. The public plates stood in three stacks beside the sink. Without the guests the palace sounded much larger.
“Julian is going,” Blaise said.
Erasmus set down his spoon.
“Did he tell you?”
“He said he thought he would. I saw him take the cart west.”
“Then he may be.”

Blaise had expected the patron to correct the tense. He might have said that Julian would come back, that the departure belonged to an afternoon which need not determine anything. Instead he moved a second bowl toward him.
The soup was too hot. Blaise ate it anyway. He wanted to finish something.
“I said a line,” he told Erasmus. “One we wrote together. He hadn't written it here yet.”
“Ah.”
“He thinks I took something from him.”
“Did you?”
“I remembered it.”
“That is not always the whole answer.”
Blaise set down the spoon.
“You could have told me that earlier.”
“I believe I have told you many things earlier.”
The patron reached for bread, and Blaise saw him discover that there was none left. He looked disappointed in a plain, bodily way. It made Blaise angry that he should still be able to want bread.
“You remember everything,” Blaise said. “You know what he wanted before this.”
“I remember more of it than you do.”
“Then you know this isn't all he is.”
“Of course it isn't.”

That assent was dangerously pleasant. Blaise found himself able to sit more comfortably. Julian's present refusal could be one incomplete expression of a life whose complete meaning was held elsewhere. A finite answer, corrected by a more comprehensive love.
He noticed that he had given Erasmus the position from which Julian could be overruled. He also noticed that he did not want to stand up.

choices.label: Ask what the restored morning could give them.

paragraphs: Erasmus was eating in the kitchen. The public plates stood in three stacks beside the sink. Without the guests the palace sounded much larger.
“The afternoon has been ruined,” Blaise said.
Erasmus set down his spoon.
“What happened?”
“Julian thinks he will leave. I saw him take the cart west.”
“Then he may be.”

Blaise had expected the patron to correct the tense. He might have said that Julian would come back, that the departure belonged to an afternoon which need not determine anything. Instead he moved a second bowl toward him.
The soup was too hot. Blaise ate it anyway. He wanted to finish something.

“Ah.”
“He thinks I took something from him.”

He noticed that he had given Erasmus the position from which Julian could be overruled. He also noticed that he did not want to stand up.

scenes.title: What a favor can do
paragraphs: “You could be together,” Erasmus said. “You would not be obliged to make the same mistakes.”
“Would he want me?”
“He did.”
“That isn't what I asked.”
The patron wiped the rim of his bowl with a piece of cloth.
“What would satisfy you? A word which had no relation to anything he had ever known? A gesture from a man who had no reason to distinguish you from the chair?”
“You know what I mean.”
“Yes. I do.”
His voice had become less patient. Blaise was relieved. Perfect patience would have made it impossible to believe he was being heard.
“I want it to be him,” Blaise said. “When he answers. I don't want to put the words in him.”
“You can meet him. You can let him answer.”
“And if I remember the answer?”
“You remember many things about him. Would you prefer to be a stranger?”

Blaise did not. He wanted all the intimacy of a history without the power by which knowing it might alter what followed. The demand moved away whenever he approached it. If Julian were made indifferent to all their shared life, Blaise would be the first to call that a mutilation.

The bridge had not been an argument. It had fallen. He remembered the little patch of white sky between Julian's fingers, the weight of a body becoming impossible to inhabit, the certainty that there would be no opportunity to become more understanding. Julian had asked. Erasmus had answered. Afterward they had sat on the repaired stone eating bread, and for a while existing had been enough.
He could not make that goodness disappear merely because the gift had since become useful to a less admirable wish.
“I can give you the morning,” Erasmus said. “I cannot promise that you will never have a reason to ask again.”
Blaise looked toward the kitchen window. The low darkness was beginning to touch the highest streets. A woman on an upper terrace lifted a sheet clear of it and brought her washing inside.
He could still go west. He could still follow the cart.
He moved his chair closer to Erasmus.

choices.label: Ask Erasmus to restore the dedication morning, keeping your memory as witness.

scenes.title: The bowl
paragraphs: “Give me the morning,” Blaise said.
Erasmus reached for his hand. It was not a necessary gesture; he had told Blaise that before. He liked someone to be beside him.

The low darkness lifted from the upper houses. It did not move like cloud. For an instant Blaise could see the streets through it, each window occupying two positions, the familiar room and the room from which it had descended. The plate stacks made a sound like a row of teeth closing.

A bowl near Blaise's elbow had a crack across its lip. The two edges approached one another until the dark line was a hair, then an uncertainty in the glaze, then nothing. He touched the place. It was cool.
People in the square began sentences which their mouths had once begun. Somewhere a child complained about a ribbon. The voice arrived with such familiar force that Blaise almost answered it.
Then there was simply morning.
Erasmus sat beside him. The soup had gone. A pot of uncooked beans stood on the far counter.

Blaise was hungry in a different way. His body had been returned to the day's beginning, while the previous evening remained accessible with an intimacy no surviving object in the kitchen appeared to share.
“You should go to him,” Erasmus said.
The advice sounded generous. Blaise got up before he could ask whether he would have thought so yesterday.
Across the square, the theatre window stood open. There was no movement behind it.

choices.label: Cross the square and look for Julian.

sources.title: Before the first witnessed return: Erasmus's promise
sources.text: Erasmus canceled the public address when Blaise refused it, took down the cloth, and told him that while Blaise remains in Aubade he will not restore the city without Blaise's request.

sources.title: Before the first witnessed return: the westbound cart
sources.text: Blaise saw Julian walking with the cart and the painted door. It continued onto the west road rather than turning toward Vera's instruments.

sources.title: The first witnessed return: the restored bowl
sources.text: After Blaise asked for the dedication morning, he and Erasmus remained together while the cracked bowl became whole, the soup disappeared and the city resumed its morning conditions. Blaise retained his memory of the preceding evening.

notes.source: Opening sample paragraphs are retained verbatim from the reviewed bec72856 sample; new surrounding scenes are authored for this complete production.
notes.actors: The first return changes Vera to vera-witness when she is encountered again. Julian was outside and remains julian. Blaise retains memory until the second return.
